title: Don't come near, I'm on fire
takeaway: Don't take away the ache; it's the only thing I have left of you.
scene: The poet warns people away. He is burning with the pain of being separated from someone he loves, and he doesn't want the fire to spread. By the end he is speaking straight to God.

original: میں ہاں اگ ہجر دا سڑیا میرے کول نہ آؤ
بچ سکو تے بھانبڑ کولوں اپنا آپ بچاؤ
transliteration: Main haan agg hijr da sariya, mere kol na aao
Bach sako te bhaambar kolon apna aap bachaao
translation: I've been burned by the fire of separation; don't come near me.
If you can escape it, save yourself from this blaze.
couplets.story: He tells everyone to keep their distance. Missing someone has set him on fire, and he doesn't want it to spread. If you can, stay away and save yourself.

original: کتھے دل دے دکھڑے پھولاں کتھے بھار اتاراں
وچھڑ گئے جو دل دے جانی کدھروں ڈھونڈ لیاؤ
transliteration: Kitthe dil de dukhre pholaan, kitthe bhaar utaaraan
Vichhar gaye jo dil de jaani, kidhron dhoondh liaao
translation: Where can I open up my heart's sorrows? Where can I set down this weight?
Find the dear one of my heart, who left me, and bring them back from somewhere.
couplets.story: He has nowhere to share his pain and nowhere to put down this heavy load. He begs people to find the one he lost, wherever they are, and bring them back.

original: سدھراں دا چن اک تیلا آہلنا کسے بنایا
ایہنوں کیوں اڈاون لگی او جھکھڑی تیز ہواؤ
transliteration: Sadhraan da chun ik teela aahlna kise banaaya
Ehnu kyon udaavan lagi o jhakhri tez havaao
translation: Someone built a nest from hopes, picking it twig by twig.
O fierce, stormy winds, why are you blowing it away?
couplets.story: His hopes were like a bird's nest, built one twig at a time. Now storm winds are blowing it apart, and he asks why.

original: مشتاقاں نے رولا پایا صنم ماہی نے لنگھنا
میرے وی گل جنجو پاؤ، متھے تلک تے لگاؤ
transliteration: Mushtaaqaan ne rola paaya, sanam maahi ne langhna
Mere vi gal janjoo paao, matthe tilak te lagaao
translation: The eager ones raised a shout: 'The beloved idol is coming by!'
Then put a sacred thread round my neck too, and a tilak mark on my forehead.
couplets.story: Word goes round that the beloved will pass by, and all the admirers get excited. The poet jokes about it. If the beloved is worshipped like an idol, he might as well dress like a temple worshipper too, with the sacred thread and the mark on his forehead.

original: ایسی رات غماں دی کالی شائد پوہ نہ پھٹے
شمع اپنے پیار دی میرے دل وچ آن جلاؤ
transliteration: Aisi raat ghamaan di kaali, shaayad poh na phatte
Shamaa apne pyaar di mere dil vich aan jalaao
translation: This night of sorrow is so dark, maybe dawn will never break.
Come and light the candle of your love in my heart.
couplets.story: His sadness feels like a night so dark that morning might never come. He asks the beloved to come and light a candle of love inside his heart.

original: تر گئے عاشق جیہڑے ہتھیں محبوباں نے ڈوبے
میں وی امر ہو جاواں جیکر زہر دا جام پلاؤ
transliteration: Tar gaye aashiq jehre hatthin mehbooban ne dobe
Main vi amar ho jaavaan jekar zehar da jaam pilaao
translation: The lovers drowned by their beloveds' own hands were the ones who reached the shore.
I too would become immortal, if you gave me a cup of poison to drink.
couplets.story: Here is a strange truth. The lovers who were 'drowned' by the ones they loved are the ones who really made it across. So if the beloved handed him a cup of poison, he'd drink it, and it would make him live forever.

original: اک تھک تے رو کرلا کے ہجر دا روگی ستا اے
ہن تے ایہدا پیار دی سدھر و بوہا نہ کھڑکاؤ
transliteration: Ik thak te ro karla ke hijr da rogi sutta ae
Hun te ehda pyaar di sadhro, boha na kharkaao
translation: Worn out from weeping and wailing, the one sick with separation has fallen asleep.
O longings of love, don't knock on his door now.
couplets.story: After crying for so long, the lovesick man has finally fallen asleep from exhaustion. He asks his own longings: please, don't knock on the door and wake him.

original: لوکاں نوں مٹ بھر بھر دیو چلی چلی اے سانوں
کجھ تے خوف خدا دا کھاؤ ویلے دے خداؤ
transliteration: Lokaan nu matt bhar bhar deo, chuli chuli ae saanu
Kujh te khauf Khuda da khaao, vele de khudaao
translation: You give others whole jars full, and to me just a handful at a time.
Have some fear of God, you who act like the gods of this age.
couplets.story: He turns to the powerful people of his time. They hand out plenty to others, but give him only scraps. He reminds them: you act like you're gods, but you should fear the real God.

original: سوز فراق تیرے نہ چھڈیا کجھ احمدؔ دے پلے
اپنی نظر کرم دی دولت ایہدی جھولی پاؤ
transliteration: Soz-e-firaaq tere na chhadiya kujh Ahmad de palle
Apni nazar-e-karam di daulat ehdi jholi paao
translation: The burning of separation from You has left Ahmad with nothing.
Pour the treasure of Your kind glance into his lap.
couplets.story: He ends with a prayer. Being apart from the Beloved has left him with nothing at all. So he asks for one gift: a kind look, which would be worth more than any treasure.

deeper:
The last two couplets make the poem's direction clear. 'Have some fear of God, you gods of this age' is a rebuke to people who behave as if they were powerful. The final prayer for a 'glance of kindness' (nazar-e-karam) is the classic Sufi request to God, or to a saint, for grace.

'The lovers drowned by their beloveds' own hands reached the shore' is a Sufi paradox. Those who let go of themselves in God are the ones who are saved. The joke about the sacred thread and tilak mark, symbols of Hindu worship, says that love doesn't care about outward labels. Bulleh Shah made that theme famous.
why: It moves from personal heartbreak to a jab at people with power, and ends in a prayer. That journey is typical of this book.
prompt: Is there someone with power over you who forgets that they will answer to God too? How do you handle that?
notes: Couplet 4: the 'janjoo' (sacred thread) and 'tilak' are Hindu marks of worship. This is a deliberately provocative image in the Bulleh Shah tradition, not a literal statement of belief.
Couplet 6, line 1: 'tar gaye' can mean 'were saved / crossed over'; the paradox depends on it.
